title: Where MetroVolt Stands Today
lede: MetroVolt is a design and simulation study of the Kronos burner — no MetroVolt unit has been built, and no net-power hardware exists yet.
body: MetroVolt is the data-center and city housing of the Kronos burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), a D-³He tandem-mirror generator. It shares the same core as Aegis: a 26.49 T plug, a 17 T throat, a neutron fraction near 5.44%, and direct energy conversion. Today that machine exists as physics models, reproducible simulations, and engineering studies — not as operating hardware.

The Kronos program builds the breeder (Hyperion) first. Breeder construction begins Q2 2027, with first-of-a-kind first tritium near 2030. The burner follows as a test unit near 2032, with a commercial fleet targeted near 2036. MetroVolt is perfected in simulation while the breeder is built.
What we claim, and what we do not

We claim a computed, reproducible design point and a credible development path. We do not claim a demonstrated net-electric burner, a built MetroVolt unit, or that any date is guaranteed. Where physics or engineering is unresolved, we say so on the relevant page.
Design stage: models and simulation, not built hardware.
Sequenced behind the breeder, which carries first construction risk.
Test burner near 2032; commercial fleet near 2036.
Open items in confinement, high-field magnets, DEC, materials, and fuel supply.
Nothing on this site is an operating result. Every MetroVolt figure is a design or simulation value pending experimental confirmation.

title: What “Design Stage” Means
lede: Design stage means the machine is fully specified in physics and engineering models and reproduced in simulation, but not yet fabricated or operated.
body: A fusion generator passes through distinct maturity phases: concept, design, integrated test, and commercial build. MetroVolt is in the design phase. The plasma physics, magnet requirements, and direct-energy-conversion chain are specified as a self-consistent design point, checked in code, and documented so others can reproduce the numbers.

Design stage is not a sketch. It means a chosen operating point — 26.49 T plug field, 17 T throat, D-³He fuel, a neutron fraction near 5.44% — with each figure traced to a model. What it is not is a built machine: no MetroVolt plasma has been struck, and no direct-conversion module has produced grid power.

Calling a design a demonstration is how fusion loses trust. MetroVolt figures are design and simulation values. The test unit near 2032 is where those values first meet hardware, and where the design either holds or is revised.
Specified: operating point, magnets, fuel cycle, DEC chain.
Simulated: plasma, power balance, thermal and neutron loads.
Not yet done: fabrication, integrated operation, net-power demonstration.
The rest of this section walks the path from this design stage to a commercial fleet, and names the gates that must be cleared along the way.

title: Simulation Study, Not Built Hardware
lede: MetroVolt’s numbers come from reproducible simulation — valuable for design, but not a substitute for an experiment.
body: What a simulation can and cannot settle

MetroVolt’s design point is produced by physics and engineering codes: plasma equilibrium and confinement models, power-balance calculations, magnet and structural analysis, and a direct-energy-conversion model. These are reproducible — the inputs and code produce the same outputs on a clean machine — which is the standard we hold ourselves to.

Simulation is strong at exploring a design space, ranking options, and finding where a concept breaks. It is weak wherever the model is incomplete: turbulent transport at the plug, wall and material behavior under a real neutron spectrum, and integrated plant dynamics. Those are exactly the items the test unit exists to measure.

No amount of computation demonstrates net power; only an integrated machine does. The honest reading of MetroVolt today is: the design is self-consistent in simulation, and several assumptions carry real uncertainty that only hardware resolves.
Reproducible: same code and inputs give the same design point.
Explored: sensitivity to field, density, temperature, and geometry.
Unproven by simulation alone: confinement margin, materials life, net electric output.
Treat every MetroVolt performance number as a simulation prediction until a test unit measures it.

title: The Honest Gates Between Here and Power
lede: A short list of physics and engineering gates stands between the MetroVolt design and a firm-power fleet — named plainly, not buried.
body: Rather than a single confidence number, the honest picture is a set of gates. Each is a question the design must answer with hardware, not argument. Some are partially addressed by the breeder program; others are specific to the burner.

Open means the answer is genuinely unknown and could revise the design. Partial means related work exists (in the breeder program or the wider field) but the burner-specific case is unproven. Design means the approach is specified and simulated but not built.
No gate is closed by claiming it is closed.
The test unit near 2032 is where the first-order gates are measured.
Dates move before physics does — if a gate fails, the schedule yields.
Each gate has its own page in this section with the specific question, the current basis, and what would count as passing it.

title: The Timeline at a Glance
lede: Breeder construction Q2 2027, breeder first tritium ~2030, burner test unit ~2032, commercial fleet ~2036 — the plan, not a promise.
body: MetroVolt sits inside a two-machine program. The breeder is built first because it delivers value on fusion gain alone; the burner follows once the breeder has retired first construction and operations risk. The dates below are targets from the current plan.

The years between milestones are not idle. Breeder construction and early operation feed magnet, cryogenics, tritium-handling, and controls experience directly into the burner. The burner test unit is designed and long-lead hardware ordered while the breeder runs, so 2032 is a build-and-test date, not a start-from-scratch date.

No MetroVolt performance claim precedes its test unit. There is no hardware net-gain claim before the breeder’s first-of-a-kind milestone, and no commercial burner claim before the 2032 test unit reports.
Every date here is a plan target. A failed gate moves the date; it does not get waved through.

title: Why the Breeder Comes First
lede: The breeder reaches useful output on fusion gain alone; the burner must clear net electric, a harder bar — so the breeder is built first.
body: Kronos develops a breeder (Hyperion), a compact D-T spherical tokamak, and a burner (Aegis / MetroVolt), a D-³He tandem-mirror generator. They differ in what each must demonstrate before delivering value, and that difference sets the build order.

The breeder’s product is material: a tritium-class output near 4 kg/yr, a helium-3 coproduct near 1.97 kg/yr, and 14 MeV neutrons. Delivering those needs fusion gain (Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW fusion power) — not net electricity. The burner’s product is electricity, which requires net electric output: gross power minus everything recirculated to magnets, heating, and cryogenics must stay positive. That is the harder threshold.

Building the breeder first retires shared risk — high-field magnets, cryogenics, tritium handling, plasma control, and construction — before the burner attempts the harder net-electric goal. It also produces the helium-3 coproduct relevant to D-³He fuel.
Breeder: value on gain; first construction risk carried here.
Burner: value on net electric; sequenced after breeder de-risking.
Shared learning: magnets, cryo, controls, and manufacturing transfer forward.
MetroVolt therefore matures in simulation and design while the breeder is built, ready for a test unit once the breeder has proven the foundations.

title: What the Breeder Proves for the Burner
lede: The breeder program de-risks magnets, cryogenics, controls, manufacturing, and helium-3 supply — each of which the burner inherits.
body: The burner does not start from zero in 2032. The breeder’s construction and operation from 2027 onward produce concrete, transferable results. The handoff is the reason the burner test unit is credible on that timeline.

Some burner physics is genuinely new. The tandem-mirror confinement, the 26.49 T plug, and direct energy conversion have no breeder analogue and must be proven on the burner’s own path. The breeder reduces engineering and operational risk; it does not resolve the burner’s core confinement question.
Transfers well: magnets, cryogenics, controls, tritium handling.
Transfers partly: manufacturing scale, helium-3 supply.
Does not transfer: tandem-mirror confinement, plug field, DEC.
This is why the burner has its own gate list even after the breeder succeeds — shared foundations, distinct core physics.

title: The Test Burner, ~2032
lede: Near 2032 the Kronos burner core is built as an integrated test unit — the first time MetroVolt physics meets hardware.
body: The purpose of the test unit

The ~2032 test burner is the first integrated D-³He tandem-mirror machine in the Kronos program. Its job is to measure, not to sell power: does the plug confine at feasible β, does the 26.49 T field hold, does direct energy conversion work on real particles, and how do materials behave at a neutron fraction near 5.44%.

It carries the same core as both burner housings — Aegis (fixed defense installations) and MetroVolt (data centers and cities). The housings differ; the physics under test is shared, so a single test unit informs both products.

Success is not a headline number. It is a set of measurements that either confirm the design point or reveal where it must change. A confirmed confinement margin and a working direct-conversion chain would be the strongest results; a shortfall would revise the design before any fleet commitment.
Measures confinement, plug field, DEC efficiency, materials response.
Informs both Aegis and MetroVolt housings.
Gates the commercial decision — no fleet without its results.
The test unit is where MetroVolt stops being a simulation. Until it reports, every burner performance figure remains a prediction.

title: Commercial Availability, ~2036
lede: A commercial MetroVolt fleet is targeted near 2036 — conditional on the ~2032 test unit clearing its gates.
body: From one test to a fleet

Commercial availability near 2036 means MetroVolt units built to serve data centers and cities with firm power. This target is explicitly conditional: it follows only if the ~2032 test unit confirms confinement, field, direct energy conversion, and materials life, and if helium-3 fuel supply is on a credible footing.
Why 2036, and why it can move

The four years between test and fleet cover design finalization, first-of-a-kind build, and the next-of-a-kind refinement that follows. If the test unit reveals a shortfall, this window absorbs a redesign-and-retest loop, and the date moves. The date is a plan, not a commitment independent of results.
Conditional on 2032 test-unit results across all first-order gates.
Covers FOAK build then NOAK refinement.
Slips if a gate fails — physics is not negotiated against a calendar.
MetroVolt’s value proposition — firm 24/7 power co-located with load, with almost no water — is a design property, not a demonstrated fleet property, until commercial units operate.
No commercial firm-power claim precedes an operating commercial unit. 2036 is the target for that unit, not proof of it.

title: FOAK, NOAK, BOAK Explained
lede: First-, next-, and buy-of-a-kind name the build stages: the first integrated unit, its refined successor, and fleet units carrying the learning.
body: Fusion programs, like other first-of-their-kind infrastructure, improve build-to-build. Kronos names the stages FOAK, NOAK, and BOAK to keep the maturity honest — a first unit is not a fleet unit, and should not be described as one.
FOAK — first-of-a-kind: the first integrated commercial build, carrying the most uncertainty and the fewest completed learnings.
NOAK — next-of-a-kind: the second builds, incorporating what FOAK taught about fabrication, assembly, and operation.
BOAK — buy-of-a-kind: fleet units built with a stabilized design and mature supply chain.
The breeder walks this ladder first (FOAK first tritium ~2030, then NOAK and BOAK). The burner walks its own ladder after the ~2032 test unit, with a commercial FOAK on the path to a fleet near 2036.

Performance and reliability legitimately differ across these stages. A FOAK unit may need more maintenance and show more variability than a BOAK unit. Naming the stage keeps any performance figure attached to the maturity it actually reflects.
MetroVolt fleet properties — firmness, availability, small water footprint at scale — are BOAK expectations, validated stepwise from FOAK onward.

title: Technology Readiness Levels
lede: On a nine-level readiness scale, MetroVolt’s design and validated simulation place it near TRL 3–4, with the test unit targeting TRL 6–7.
body: Technology Readiness Levels (TRL 1–9) are a widely used maturity scale, from basic principles (TRL 1) through validated components (TRL 4–5), integrated demonstration (TRL 6–7), to a proven operational system (TRL 8–9). Applying it to MetroVolt keeps claims proportionate.

A specified design point with reproducible simulation and analytical validation is consistent with TRL 3–4: the concept is formulated and key parameters are validated in models, but not in an integrated environment. The ~2032 test unit is designed to advance the burner core toward TRL 6–7 by demonstrating an integrated machine in a relevant environment.
TRL 1–2: principles and concept — established for D-³He tandem mirrors.
TRL 3–4: analytical and simulation validation — MetroVolt today.
TRL 6–7: integrated demonstration — the ~2032 test-unit target.
TRL 8–9: qualified, operational system — the commercial fleet goal.

TRL is a coarse instrument and different subsystems sit at different levels — magnets and cryogenics benefit from breeder work, while tandem-mirror confinement and direct energy conversion are less mature. The gate pages give the subsystem-specific picture.

title: The Plug-Density Open Item
lede: The central open physics question is whether the tandem-mirror plug confines the plasma at a feasible operating point — unresolved today.
body: A tandem-mirror generator confines plasma between two high-field magnetic plugs. MetroVolt’s design uses a 26.49 T plug and a 17 T throat. The core open item is whether the plug provides adequate confinement — sufficient plug density and potential to hold the central-cell plasma — at a plasma pressure (β) that is actually feasible to build and sustain.

This is the single most consequential gate for the burner. If the plug requires conditions beyond what the magnets and heating can deliver, the design point changes. We flag this as genuinely open: it is not resolved by the current simulation, and it is a candidate to revise the concept.

Simulation narrows the plausible range but cannot settle it. The ~2032 test unit is the instrument: it measures confinement directly at the burner’s scale. A pass confirms the operating point; a shortfall sends the design back with concrete data.
This is an open item, stated as such. MetroVolt’s firm-power promise rests on this gate, and it is not yet cleared.

title: The Magnetic-Well Question
lede: Tandem mirrors need a stable configuration at useful plasma pressure; whether a sufficient magnetic well exists at feasible β is unresolved.
body: Magnetic confinement must be stable: the plasma should sit in an effective magnetic well so that pressure-driven instabilities do not eject it. In a tandem mirror this is achieved through field shaping. The open question is whether a configuration provides an adequate well at the plasma pressure (β) MetroVolt needs for useful output.

High β is desirable for power density but stresses stability; low β is easier to stabilize but reduces output. The design must find a point that is both stable and productive. Whether that point exists at feasible field and geometry is part of the same open question as plug confinement.
Why simulation is not the last word

Stability at the relevant pressure involves kinetic and geometric effects that models capture imperfectly. This is a measure-it question. The test unit is built precisely to observe whether the configuration holds at the intended β.
Need: a stable well at a productive β.
Risk: no feasible point that is both stable and high-output.
Resolution: direct measurement on the ~2032 test unit.
Until then, MetroVolt treats the stable-well assumption as a design premise under test, not a settled fact.

title: The 26.49 T Plug-Magnet Gate
lede: MetroVolt’s plug needs a 26.49 T field and the throat 17 T — at the frontier of high-field superconducting magnets, partially de-risked by the breeder.
body: The burner design calls for a 26.49 T plug field and a 17 T throat field. These are high even by modern high-temperature-superconductor standards. Building magnets that reach and hold these fields reliably, with the forces and quench protection they imply, is a serious engineering gate.

This gate is partial, not open: the breeder (Hyperion) program develops high-field superconducting magnets (its own peak field is 16.84 T, 8 T on-axis) and the cryogenics to run them. That experience transfers directly. The burner still pushes further, so the plug magnet remains a first-order engineering item.

Passing means a plug magnet that reaches 26.49 T, tolerates the structural loads, protects against quench, and runs for realistic durations — first as a prototype, then integrated in the ~2032 test unit.
Requirement: 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, sustained and safe.
Basis: breeder high-field magnet and cryogenics experience.
Remaining: the incremental step to plug-class fields at the burner.
High field is an engineering gate with a real head start from the breeder — credible, but not yet demonstrated at plug class.

title: Direct-Energy-Conversion Efficiency Gate
lede: MetroVolt replaces the steam turbine with direct energy conversion; whether it reaches useful efficiency at scale is a design-stage gate.
body: Direct energy conversion (DEC) captures the kinetic energy of charged fusion products and decelerates them against an electric field, delivering current without a thermal cycle. In a D-³He burner, most fusion energy appears in charged particles, which makes DEC attractive — and makes its efficiency central to the machine’s value.

The gate is whether DEC reaches a useful conversion efficiency in an integrated machine, handling the real particle spectrum, space-charge limits, and thermal loads on the collector. The approach is specified and simulated; it is at design stage, not demonstrated at generator scale.
Why DEC matters for MetroVolt specifically

DEC is the reason MetroVolt needs almost no water: with no steam cycle there is little to cool by evaporation. It is also central to net electric output, since conversion efficiency directly sets how much of the fusion power reaches the grid. A DEC shortfall would weaken both the water story and the power story.
Captures charged-particle energy without a turbine.
Removes the steam cycle — hence the small water footprint.
Efficiency at scale is a design-stage gate, measured on the test unit.
DEC is specified and simulated. Its at-scale efficiency is a prediction until the ~2032 test unit converts real particles to current.

title: The 5.44% Neutron Fraction and Materials
lede: D-³He is mostly aneutronic, but a neutron fraction near 5.44% still loads the first wall — material life at that flux is a qualification gate.
body: D-³He fusion is chosen partly because it produces far fewer neutrons than D-T. But it is not neutron-free: side reactions (notably D-D) give the burner a neutron fraction near 5.44%. That fraction is small relative to a breeder, yet large enough to activate and damage first-wall and structural materials over time.

The gate is qualifying materials that survive the burner’s neutron spectrum and heat loads for a useful service life. This is partial: the breeder program and the wider field advance fusion materials, and the burner’s lower fraction eases the problem — but burner-specific qualification is not complete.

It requires material data under the relevant fluence, models of damage and activation, and test-unit exposure to confirm predicted life. The lower fraction is an advantage, not a pass — the wall still needs a demonstrated service life.
Wall and structure still activate and degrade over time.
Qualification uses breeder and field data plus test-unit exposure.
The small neutron fraction eases the materials problem; it does not remove it. First-wall life is a qualification gate.

title: The Helium-3 Supply Gate
lede: MetroVolt burns D-³He, so it needs helium-3 — scarce on Earth. Fleet-scale supply, including a lunar path, is an open program-level gate.
body: MetroVolt’s fuel is deuterium and helium-3. Deuterium is abundant. Helium-3 is not — it is scarce on Earth, available in small quantities from tritium decay and other limited sources. A single test unit can be fueled from existing supply; a commercial fleet cannot rely on that alone.

This is an open program-level gate. The breeder produces a helium-3 coproduct (near 1.97 kg/yr class), which contributes but does not by itself supply a large fleet. A credible fleet path considers lunar helium-3, which is a long-horizon source (roughly 2038–2040 in program planning) rather than a near-term one.
Why this gates the fleet, not the test

Fuel scarcity does not block the ~2032 test unit, which needs relatively little. It gates the fleet: many MetroVolt units burning D-³He imply a supply chain that does not fully exist today. Honest planning treats fleet-scale helium-3 as an unresolved dependency.
Helium-3 supply is open at fleet scale. The lunar path is a long-horizon dependency, not a solved input.

title: D-³He Fuel-Cycle Readiness
lede: Beyond sourcing helium-3, MetroVolt needs fuel processing, injection, and recovery proven — partly inherited from the breeder, partly burner-specific.
body: A working fuel cycle is not just having helium-3. It is storing, purifying, injecting, and recovering fuel; handling deuterium; and managing the small tritium and neutron activation the burner produces. Each step must be reliable for a machine expected to deliver firm power continuously.

Parts of this are de-risked by the breeder, whose D-T fuel cycle demands mature tritium handling and gas processing. The deuterium and helium-3 handling for the burner draws on that experience, though the D-³He mix and DEC-based machine differ enough to need burner-specific work.

At design stage the fuel cycle is specified and draws on breeder-adjacent maturity for most steps. The weak point is fleet-scale helium-3 resupply, covered in its own gate. The processing and injection chain will be proven on the ~2032 test unit.
Specified fuel-handling chain, breeder-adjacent for most steps.
Open dependency: fleet-scale helium-3, addressed separately.
The fuel cycle is design-stage. Injection, recovery, and processing meet hardware on the test unit.

title: Extrapolation Risk: Few Points to a Fleet
lede: Moving from a handful of test results to a fleet design carries extrapolation risk — named openly and managed by staged builds.
body: A fusion program cannot build hundreds of prototypes. It measures a few machines and extrapolates to a fleet. That extrapolation is a real risk: behavior that holds at test scale may shift at fleet scale or across many units, and a design tuned to a couple of data points can be over-fit.

MetroVolt inherits this risk twice — once from the breeder’s own few-unit ladder, and once from the burner’s. Program documentation flags a specific two-point-to-fleet extrapolation concern, which is why the FOAK–NOAK–BOAK ladder exists: to add data points before committing to a fleet design.

The mitigation is staged builds with instrumentation, conservative margins where data is thin, and a willingness to revise the design between stages. Each build is treated as a measurement, not just a delivery, so the extrapolation shortens with every unit.
Risk: over-fitting a fleet design to few test points.
Mitigation: staged FOAK→NOAK→BOAK with measurement at each step.
Discipline: margins where data is thin; revise between stages.
Extrapolation from few units to a fleet is an acknowledged risk, not a solved problem. Staged builds shrink it; they do not erase it.

title: How We Validate Before Building
lede: MetroVolt is validated in layers — code verification, physics validation, digital twin, then hardware — so that each build tests specific predictions.
body: Validation is not one act but a sequence. Each layer catches different errors: code verification checks the math is solved correctly, physics validation checks the models match known experiments, the digital twin integrates them into a machine-level prediction, and hardware tests the whole against reality.

The point of validation is to enter each hardware step with specific, falsifiable predictions. The ~2032 test unit is not an open-ended experiment; it checks named predictions about confinement, field, DEC efficiency, and materials. Where measurement disagrees with prediction, the models are corrected before the next build.
Verify the code, validate the physics, integrate in the twin, test in hardware.
Feed disagreements back into the models between builds.
This layered approach is why MetroVolt calls itself a design and simulation study today, and why the honest gates are stated before, not after, the hardware.

title: Verification & Validation of the Codes
lede: MetroVolt’s codes are verified for correctness and validated against known data — the standard that lets a design point be trusted as a prediction.
body: Verification asks: are we solving the equations right? Validation asks: are we solving the right equations — do they match reality? Both are needed. A code can be perfectly verified and still wrong about the world, or physically reasonable but numerically broken.

MetroVolt’s design point is produced by codes held to reproducibility: the same inputs and code produce the same outputs on a clean machine, with a documented environment. That is the floor for verification. Validation compares model outputs against known tandem-mirror and plasma data where it exists.

Validation is strongest where relevant experimental data exists and weakest exactly at the burner’s novel physics — plug confinement at feasible β and direct energy conversion at scale. Those thin areas are the honest gates, and the reason the design is not treated as settled.
Validation: strong where data exists, thin at novel physics.
Gaps map exactly onto the open items and the test-unit plan.
A verified, partly validated design is a strong prediction — not a demonstration. The gaps are named, not hidden.

title: The Digital Twin in the Path
lede: A predictive digital twin integrates MetroVolt’s models into a machine-level simulation used to design, plan tests, and later to operate.
body: Individual codes model pieces — plasma, magnets, DEC, thermal loads. A digital twin integrates them into a single predictive model of the whole machine. For MetroVolt at design stage, the twin is where subsystem models are made consistent and where machine-level behavior is explored before any metal is cut.

The twin serves three roles across the timeline: it sharpens the design now, it plans and interprets the ~2032 test unit, and it becomes an operational tool once hardware exists — running alongside the machine to predict, control, and diagnose.

A digital twin is only as good as its models. It does not confirm physics on its own; it inherits every uncertainty in its inputs, including the open confinement and DEC questions. Its value is disciplined integration and fast exploration, not proof. The test unit remains the arbiter.
Integrates subsystem models into a machine-level prediction.
Designs now, plans the test, operates later.
Carries — does not resolve — the underlying physics uncertainty.
The twin is a central tool of the design stage and a bridge to operations, which is why it appears throughout the readiness path.

title: Open Physics Questions
lede: The burner’s open physics reduces to a few named questions — plug confinement, magnetic-well stability, and DEC behavior — each honestly unresolved.
body: The physics that must be proven

MetroVolt rests on physics that is credible in design but not yet demonstrated at generator scale. Rather than a single confidence figure, the honest picture is a short list of specific questions, each with a clear pass condition and each resolvable only by the test unit.

Naming open physics is a credibility choice. A program that lists only successes hides its risks; MetroVolt lists the questions so that any performance claim can be read against what remains unproven. The two confinement items are the load-bearing ones — if either fails, the design point changes materially.
Load-bearing: plug confinement and magnetic-well stability.
Partial: neutron-fraction spectrum, aided by breeder and field data.
These are open questions, stated as open. MetroVolt’s promise is conditional on answering them with hardware.

title: Open Engineering Questions
lede: Beyond physics, MetroVolt has engineering gates — plug magnets, cryogenics, DEC hardware, materials, and integration — at varying maturity.
body: Even with the physics proven, a firm-power machine must be engineered: magnets built and protected, cryogenics run continuously, direct-conversion collectors handling real loads, materials qualified, and everything integrated into a reliable plant. These are the engineering gates, several of them helped by the breeder.

Magnets, cryogenics, and materials benefit from the breeder and the wider field, so they are partial rather than open. DEC collectors and full plant integration are burner-specific and sit at design — specified and simulated, awaiting the test unit. None is demonstrated at MetroVolt scale.
Head start: magnets, cryogenics, materials (from the breeder).
All meet hardware on the ~2032 test unit.
Engineering gates tend to be resolved by disciplined build-and-test, whereas physics gates can force redesign. Both are tracked in the risk register.

title: Materials Qualification Path
lede: First-wall and structural materials must be qualified for the burner’s neutron and heat loads — eased by D-³He, not eliminated.
body: Qualifying a material for a fusion machine means showing it survives the expected neutron fluence, heat flux, and chemical environment for a useful service life, with predictable degradation and activation. For MetroVolt the neutron load is modest — a fraction near 5.44% — but heat flux on DEC-facing and plasma-facing surfaces is still demanding.

Qualification proceeds from existing material databases and breeder-program data, through models of damage and activation, to exposure on the ~2032 test unit that confirms predicted life. The lower neutron fraction shortens the path relative to a D-T machine, but a demonstrated service life still requires test-unit hours.
Inputs: field data, breeder-program results, damage models.
Advantage: lower neutron fraction than D-T machines.
Still required: burner-specific life confirmed on hardware.
Lower neutron loading eases qualification; it does not complete it. Service life is proven on the test unit, not asserted.

title: Cryogenic Plant Readiness
lede: High-field superconducting magnets need continuous cryogenics; MetroVolt inherits this readiness largely from the breeder program.
body: Superconducting magnets operate at cryogenic temperatures and must stay there without interruption for a machine delivering firm power. The cryogenic plant — refrigeration, distribution, and thermal management — is therefore a readiness item in its own right, tightly coupled to the magnets it serves.

This gate is partial and well-supported. The breeder (Hyperion) runs high-field magnets (16.84 T peak) and thus develops the cryogenics to match. That plant experience transfers to the burner, whose 26.49 T plug and 17 T throat push cooling further but along a proven direction.

The incremental work is cooling higher-field magnets and sustaining the duty cycle a firm-power generator implies. This is engineering along a known path rather than new physics, which is why it is partial rather than open — but it is not yet demonstrated at burner scale.
Requirement: continuous cryogenics for plug and throat magnets.
Remaining: higher fields, firm-power duty, at the test unit.
Cryogenics readiness advances directly with the breeder, one of the clearest examples of breeder-to-burner transfer.

title: DEC Power-Electronics Readiness
lede: Direct energy conversion delivers electricity through collectors and power electronics that must handle high currents and voltages reliably.
body: Direct energy conversion produces electrical power by decelerating charged particles against an electric field. Getting that power to a data center or grid requires collectors that handle particle and heat loads, plus power electronics that condition high-current, high-voltage output into grid-compatible power — all at generator scale.

This is a burner-specific gate at design stage. Unlike magnets or cryogenics, DEC collectors and their power electronics have no direct breeder analogue, since the breeder uses fusion gain rather than net electric conversion. The chain is specified and simulated; it is not yet built at scale.

The test unit must show that collectors survive the real particle spectrum and heat flux, that space-charge limits do not cap conversion, and that power electronics deliver stable, dispatchable output. These are the pieces that turn a physics effect into firm power on-site.
Collectors: handle particle flux and heat at scale.
Power electronics: condition output to grid-compatible power.
Dispatch: stable, controllable delivery to co-located load.
The DEC power chain is design-stage and burner-specific — among the items with the least head start from the breeder.

title: Balance of Plant for a Steam-Free Machine
lede: Without a steam cycle, MetroVolt’s balance of plant is simpler in some ways and novel in others — cooling, electrical, and controls all shift.
body: Balance of plant is everything around the reactor core: cooling, electrical systems, controls, fuel handling, and safety systems. Because MetroVolt uses direct energy conversion instead of a steam turbine, its balance of plant differs from a thermal power station — no boiler, no large steam turbine, and far less cooling water.

That simplifies some subsystems and introduces others. There is no steam loop to maintain, but there is a high-power DEC output chain, cryogenics, and magnet power supplies to run continuously. The net is a plant shaped around electrical and cryogenic systems rather than thermal-hydraulic ones.

Cryogenics and magnet power draw on breeder experience; the DEC output chain is burner-specific; controls extend the breeder’s plasma-control and digital-twin work. Most balance-of-plant subsystems are conventional or breeder-adjacent, with the DEC chain as the novel element.
Removed: boiler, steam turbine, large evaporative cooling.
Added / emphasized: DEC output chain, magnet power, cryogenics.
Shared: controls and digital twin from the breeder program.
The steam-free design is the root of MetroVolt’s small water footprint, verified as its own readiness item.

title: Site-Readiness for Data Centers and Cities
lede: MetroVolt is designed to sit beside the load — a small, low-water footprint intended for data-center campuses and urban edges.
body: MetroVolt’s premise is co-location: a firm generator next to a data-center campus or at a city’s edge, delivering power over a short interconnect. That premise shapes readiness — the machine must be compact, low-water, and acceptable to site near people and critical loads.

Siting near load means meeting footprint, water, noise, and safety expectations that a remote thermal plant can avoid. The near-absence of a steam cycle helps footprint and water. The safety case, licensing, and community acceptance are separate readiness items, each in early stages appropriate to a design-stage machine.
Compact footprint suited to campus or urban-edge siting.
Almost no process water — no large cooling infrastructure.
Safety, licensing, and acceptance handled as their own gates.
Site-readiness is a property to be demonstrated, not assumed. The test unit and early commercial builds will establish real footprint, water, and interface figures against the design intent.
Co-located siting is a design goal. Real footprint and interface data come from the test unit and first builds.

title: Regulatory and Licensing Path
lede: A novel fusion generator sited near cities needs a regulatory path; Kronos pursues pre-application engagement under a byproduct-material framework.
body: Licensing a new kind of machine

Any power-producing fusion machine must be licensed to operate, and one sited near data centers or cities faces particular scrutiny. Fusion’s regulatory framework is still maturing, which makes early, honest engagement with regulators part of readiness rather than an afterthought.

Kronos approaches this through pre-application engagement, working within a byproduct-material framework appropriate to fusion devices rather than fission licensing designed for a different technology. This is early-stage: the burner is a design, and licensing follows the machine’s maturity.

No MetroVolt unit is licensed, and no site approval exists. The framework favors fusion’s lower hazard profile relative to fission, but a specific approval is earned through a documented safety case and site review, not assumed from a favorable framework.
Early engagement and framework fit are underway.
Safety case is at design stage.
Site and operating approval are future, machine-specific steps.
Licensing is early. A favorable framework is not an approval; each site is earned on its own safety case.

title: Building the Safety Case
lede: MetroVolt’s safety case rests on D-³He’s low neutron output and inherent fusion safety, documented rather than assumed.
body: Why fusion, and this fuel, helps

Fusion cannot run away: the plasma is hard to sustain, and any disturbance stops it. There is no chain reaction and no long-lived high-level waste of the fission kind. D-³He goes further, with a neutron fraction near 5.44% — far below a D-T machine — which reduces activation and shielding demands. These properties are the foundation of the safety case.

A foundation is not a finished case. Building it means documenting every hazard — magnetic energy, cryogenics, tritium byproduct, activation, high-power electronics — and showing each is controlled. At design stage this is in progress, informed by the breeder’s tritium and radiological work.

The conventional industrial hazards — stored magnetic energy, cryogens, high-power electronics — are real and must be engineered and documented like any plant. The activation and tritium-byproduct handling draw on breeder practice. The full case is completed alongside the machine, not ahead of it.
Strengths: no runaway, no fission-type waste, low neutron output.
To document: activation, tritium byproduct, industrial hazards.
Basis: breeder radiological and tritium experience.
Fusion’s inherent safety is a strong start, not a completed safety case. Each hazard is documented and controlled explicitly.

title: Supply-Chain Readiness
lede: A MetroVolt fleet depends on suppliers for high-field magnets, cryogenics, DEC hardware, and helium-3 — some mature, some to be built.
body: What a fleet needs to be built from

Delivering many MetroVolt units requires a supply chain: superconducting-magnet manufacturing, cryogenic systems, precision structures, direct-conversion hardware, power electronics, and fuel. Some of these are established industries; others, notably high-field HTS magnets at volume and helium-3 at fleet scale, are constrained.

The breeder program develops magnet and cryogenics supply first, seeding those chains before the burner needs them. That is another reason for building the breeder first — it matures shared suppliers. The burner-specific chains (DEC hardware, fleet-scale helium-3) still need deliberate development.
Constrained: high-field magnet volume, DEC hardware, helium-3.
Breeder seeds the shared magnet and cryogenics suppliers.
Supply chain is partly mature and partly to-be-built. Fleet-scale helium-3 and DEC hardware are the binding constraints.

title: Manufacturing for a Fleet
lede: Fleet-scale MetroVolt requires repeatable manufacturing of magnets, structures, and DEC modules — a step-change from one-off test hardware.
body: A test unit can be hand-built. A fleet cannot. Manufacturing readiness means repeatable, quality-controlled production of the components that make a MetroVolt — high-field magnets, precision structures, cryogenic systems, and direct-conversion modules — at a rate and consistency a fleet demands.

This maturity develops across the FOAK–NOAK–BOAK ladder. FOAK proves a component can be built at all; NOAK proves it can be built again with the lessons applied; BOAK proves it can be built repeatably. Manufacturing readiness is therefore inseparable from the build sequence.

High-field superconducting magnets are the pacing item: producing them consistently at volume is an industry still forming. Direct-conversion modules are burner-specific and have no volume precedent. Structures, cryogenics, and power electronics are more conventional. The breeder’s magnet builds seed the hardest chain.
Pacing item: high-field magnets at consistent volume.
Novel: DEC modules with no volume precedent.
Manufacturing at fleet scale is a BOAK-stage capability, proven stepwise — not a design-stage claim.

title: The Test Program, 2027–2032
lede: Between breeder construction and the burner test unit, the years 2027–2032 build shared experience and burner-specific prototypes.
body: The window between breeder construction (from Q2 2027) and the burner test unit (~2032) is a working period, not a wait. The breeder is built and begins operation; burner-specific prototypes are developed; and long-lead hardware for the test unit is designed and ordered.
2027–29 — breeder construction; magnet, cryo, and controls experience begins to accrue.
2029–31 — breeder toward first tritium (~2030); burner prototypes (plug magnet, DEC module) advance.

The prototypes matter as much as the schedule. A plug-magnet prototype de-risks the 26.49 T requirement before it is integrated; a direct-conversion module prototype tests the DEC chain in isolation before the full machine. Component prototypes fail cheaply; integrated machines fail expensively.

This program is a plan built on the breeder succeeding roughly on schedule. Breeder delays propagate to the burner, since much of the burner’s readiness is inherited. The window is where most breeder-to-burner transfer physically happens.
2027–2032 is a plan contingent on breeder progress. Prototype results, not the calendar, decide when the test unit is ready.

title: First-Plasma Milestone
lede: First plasma in the burner test unit marks the transition from simulation to operating hardware — a beginning, not a performance claim.
body: First plasma is when the burner test unit first confines a plasma in its tandem-mirror configuration. It is a genuine milestone: the machine exists, the magnets energize, and the plasma forms. But it is the start of the measurement campaign, not a demonstration of firm power.

At first plasma the machine is characterized — field profiles, plasma formation, basic confinement — against the design predictions. Discrepancies here are expected and valuable; they calibrate the models before the harder confinement and burn tests.
What it does and does not show
Shows: the machine operates and forms a plasma as configured.
Shows: first data on fields and formation vs prediction.
Does not show: sustained burn, net electric output, or firmness.

Programs sometimes over-signal first plasma. MetroVolt treats it as milestone one of several — necessary, encouraging, and far short of the confinement and direct-conversion results that actually gate the commercial decision.
First plasma proves the machine exists and runs. It is not a power result and is not treated as one.

title: Sustained-Burn Milestone
lede: Sustaining a D-³He burn at the design operating point is the milestone that tests the load-bearing confinement questions.
body: After first plasma, the decisive test is sustaining a D-³He burn at, or near, the design operating point — the plug confining the central cell at feasible β, the configuration stable, and the reaction proceeding. This milestone directly tests the open confinement and magnetic-well questions.

This is where MetroVolt’s physics is confirmed or revised. A sustained burn at the intended conditions would be the strongest evidence the design point is real; a shortfall in confinement or stability would send specific, measured feedback into the models and the design.

Everything downstream — direct energy conversion, net electric, firm power — assumes a sustained burn. Confirming it converts the load-bearing physics gates from open to measured. It is the milestone most likely to either validate the concept or force a redesign.
Tests the load-bearing plug and stability questions directly.
Pass validates the design point; shortfall drives redesign.
Prerequisite for any DEC and net-electric result.
Sustained burn is the crux milestone. Until it is measured, MetroVolt’s core physics remains an open prediction.

title: The Net-Electric Milestone
lede: Net electric — more electricity out than the machine consumes — is the burner’s defining bar, unproven anywhere in fusion today.
body: Net electric means gross electrical output exceeds everything the machine recirculates: magnets, heating, cryogenics, and balance of plant. It is a harder bar than scientific gain, and no fusion machine has demonstrated it. It is the milestone that separates a research device from a power generator.

MetroVolt is designed toward net electric via direct energy conversion, which recovers charged-particle energy efficiently. But the design intent is not a demonstration. Net electric depends on the sustained burn, the DEC efficiency, and the recirculating-power budget all landing together on real hardware.
Why we state it so plainly

Overclaiming net electric is fusion’s most common credibility failure. MetroVolt states that there is no hardware net-gain claim before the breeder’s first-of-a-kind milestone, and no burner net-electric claim before the test unit measures it. The firm-power value proposition rests on this milestone, which remains ahead.
Definition: output exceeds all recirculated power.
Status: not demonstrated by any fusion machine, MetroVolt included.
Depends on: sustained burn + DEC efficiency + power budget together.
Net electric is the defining, unproven bar. No MetroVolt firm-power claim precedes an actual net-electric measurement.

title: Demonstrating Dispatchability
lede: Firm 24/7 power means dispatchable, controllable output; MetroVolt’s dispatch behavior is a design intent to be shown on hardware.
body: MetroVolt’s promise is firm power — available around the clock and controllable to match a data center or grid. Dispatchability means the generator can hold steady output and adjust within its range on demand, without weather dependence. As a fusion generator with continuous fuel, that is a design property, subject to demonstration.

Direct energy conversion and the power-electronics chain are what make dispatch possible: they condition output and allow controlled delivery to co-located load. Whether the machine holds firm output and ramps as designed is measured once the DEC chain runs at power on the test unit and early builds.
Controllable within range to follow load.
Stable delivery through the DEC and power-electronics chain.

Dispatchability is often assumed for thermal-style plants and questioned for variable renewables. MetroVolt is designed to be firm by nature of continuous fusion plus direct conversion — but the demonstration, like net electric, waits on hardware.
Firm, dispatchable output is a design intent. Real ramp and stability figures come from the test unit and first commercial builds.

title: Verifying the Almost-No-Water Claim
lede: MetroVolt’s small water footprint follows from having no steam cycle; the claim is a design consequence to be confirmed with real plant data.
body: Thermal power stations — including most fusion concepts — boil water, drive a turbine, and reject heat, consuming large amounts of cooling water. MetroVolt uses direct energy conversion instead of a steam turbine, so it has almost no steam cycle to cool. The small water footprint is a direct consequence of that architecture, not an add-on.
What still uses water, and what does not

Almost no water is not zero water. Some heat is still rejected — from magnets, cryogenics, DEC collectors, and inefficiencies — and how that heat is managed determines the residual water use. The claim is that removing the steam cycle removes the dominant water demand, leaving a much smaller footprint suited to water-stressed sites and dense urban locations.
Removed: the large evaporative cooling of a steam cycle.
Remaining: modest heat rejection from magnets, cryo, and DEC.
Result: a footprint compatible with water-constrained siting.

As a design-stage machine, the exact water figure is a projection. The test unit and first commercial builds provide measured heat-rejection and water-use data to confirm the design consequence. The physics of the claim — no steam cycle, so no steam-cycle water — is sound; the precise number is to be measured.
The water advantage follows directly from DEC. The exact figure is confirmed with real plant data, not asserted.

title: Reliability and Availability Targets
lede: Firm power implies high availability; MetroVolt’s reliability is a fleet-stage target validated across the FOAK–NOAK–BOAK ladder.
body: A firm-power generator must run when needed — high availability, few unplanned outages, predictable maintenance. For a data center or city, availability is as important as peak output. MetroVolt’s continuous-fuel, non-weather-dependent design supports high availability in principle; achieving it in practice is a maturity question.

Reliability is not a design-stage claim. A FOAK unit will show more variability and need more maintenance than a mature BOAK unit. Availability figures are legitimately fleet-stage targets, validated stepwise as the build ladder retires failure modes and stabilizes maintenance.
FOAK: discover failure modes, establish maintenance basics.
NOAK: apply lessons, reduce unplanned outages.
BOAK: stabilized design, mature maintenance, fleet availability.

Continuous fusion and direct conversion give MetroVolt an inherent path to firmness — no fuel intermittency, no weather. But inherent capability is not demonstrated availability. The honest figure is: firmness by design, availability by maturity.
High availability is a fleet-stage target earned across FOAK→NOAK→BOAK, not a property of a first unit.

title: The Go / No-Go Decision Gates
lede: The program advances through explicit decision gates; failing a gate returns work to simulation or test rather than moving forward.
body: A credible program does not advance on momentum alone. It passes explicit go/no-go gates: the design is frozen for a build only when prior results justify it, and a build proceeds to a fleet only when its results clear the physics and engineering questions. Each gate can send work backward.
Design freeze — simulation and prototypes justify committing to the test unit.
Test-unit results — confinement, field, DEC, and materials measured against prediction.
Commercial go — net-electric and dispatch results justify a FOAK build.
Fleet go — FOAK and NOAK results justify scaling to a fleet.

The important property is symmetry: a gate that can only be passed is not a gate. If test-unit results fall short, the correct outcome is a return to simulation and redesign, and a moved date — not a waved-through commitment. This is how dates yield to physics rather than the reverse.
Where MetroVolt is on the ladder
Today MetroVolt is before the design-freeze gate — in simulation, with prototypes ahead. Every later gate is genuinely open, and each is described on its own milestone or gate page.
Gates are two-way. A no-go returns work to simulation or test; nothing is waved through on schedule pressure.

title: The Readiness Risk Register
lede: MetroVolt’s main readiness risks — confinement, high field, DEC, materials, helium-3, and scaling — mapped by likelihood and impact.
body: A risk register lists what could prevent MetroVolt from reaching firm power, and weighs each by how likely it is and how much it would matter. The highest-impact risks are the load-bearing physics questions; the highest-likelihood constraints include fuel supply. Naming them is part of the honest picture.
Plug confinement / magnetic well — high impact, unresolved: could force a design change.
Helium-3 supply — high impact at fleet scale, constrained today.
DEC efficiency — moderate: affects output and the water story.
Materials at ~5.44% neutron fraction — moderate, eased by low fraction.
Two-to-fleet scaling — moderate, managed by staged builds.

Each risk has a mitigation and a resolving event. Confinement and DEC are resolved by the test unit; helium-3 by the breeder coproduct plus longer-horizon supply; materials by qualification; scaling by the FOAK–NOAK–BOAK ladder. Mitigation reduces risk; it does not close a gate that only hardware can close.
The register is a live, honest list. High-impact physics risks are unresolved and could revise the design or the dates.

title: What Could Move the Dates
lede: The 2032 and 2036 targets depend on breeder progress, physics results, high-field magnets, and helium-3 — any of which can move them.
body: The MetroVolt timeline is a plan, and plans for first-of-their-kind machines move. Rather than defend fixed dates, it is more useful to name what would move them — so a reader can judge the schedule against real dependencies.

Most of these push dates later, not earlier. The breeder schedule is the largest single lever, because the burner’s readiness is built on breeder results. A confinement shortfall is the largest physics lever, because it can force a redesign rather than a delay. Helium-3 constrains the fleet more than the test unit.
Confinement shortfall → redesign, not just delay.
Magnet or DEC lag → later test or commercial dates.
Dates move before physics does. 2032 and 2036 are targets contingent on the dependencies above.

title: What Is Frozen vs Still Moving
lede: MetroVolt’s core physics parameters are frozen for this design; the schedule, fleet details, and unresolved gates are still moving.
body: Some things about MetroVolt are settled for the current design and used consistently across all Kronos materials; others are explicitly still in motion. Separating the two prevents both false precision and false uncertainty.
Core: 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, neutron fraction ~5.44%, D-³He fuel, direct energy conversion.
Architecture: tandem-mirror burner core shared by Aegis and MetroVolt.
Sequence: breeder first, then burner test unit, then fleet.
Fleet-scale details, siting specifics, and housing engineering.
Every open physics and engineering gate.
Frozen parameters are used exactly and not reinvented per document. Moving items are stated as targets or open questions, never as settled results.
Frozen means fixed for this design, not proven by hardware. Physics gates remain open even where parameters are frozen.

title: Developing Aegis and MetroVolt Together
lede: Aegis and MetroVolt are one burner core in two housings; developing them together means the ~2032 test unit advances both products at once.
body: Kronos’s burner is a single machine — a D-³He tandem-mirror generator with a 26.49 T plug, 17 T throat, neutron fraction near 5.44%, and direct energy conversion — offered in two housings. Aegis serves fixed defense installations; MetroVolt serves data centers and cities. The physics under development is identical.

This is efficient for readiness. Every gate the burner core must clear — confinement, high field, DEC, materials — is shared. The ~2032 test unit proves the core once, informing both products. Only the housings, interfaces, and siting differ.
Shared: the entire burner core and all core-physics gates.
Aegis-specific: fixed defense-installation requirements and siting.
MetroVolt-specific: co-location with data centers, urban siting, grid tie.

Because the housings do not change the physics, MetroVolt’s readiness tracks the burner core’s readiness. A test-unit result that validates the core validates it for both Aegis and MetroVolt; a shortfall affects both. The products diverge only after the core is proven.
Aegis and MetroVolt share one core and one set of physics gates. The test unit advances both; neither runs ahead of the shared physics.

title: Where MetroVolt Sits Relative to the Field
lede: MetroVolt is one design-stage concept among many fusion efforts; its distinguishing choices are D-³He, direct conversion, and a low water footprint.
body: Many organizations pursue fusion energy, most using D-T fuel and thermal (steam-cycle) power conversion. None has demonstrated net electric. MetroVolt sits in this landscape as a design-stage concept with distinct choices, not as a proven exception — the honest comparison is on approach, not on results, because results do not yet exist for anyone.

MetroVolt’s choices carry their own harder problems — helium-3 supply and tandem-mirror confinement chief among them — which mainstream D-T tokamak efforts do not face in the same form. It is not “ahead” or “behind” the field so much as a different bet, at a similar early maturity.
Shared with the field: no demonstrated net electric anywhere yet.
Different bet: D-³He, direct conversion, low water, co-location.
Different hard problems: helium-3 supply, tandem-mirror confinement.
Comparisons here stay on technical approach and readiness. Any performance ranking would be premature for MetroVolt or any other concept while net electric remains undemonstrated across the field.
No fusion concept, MetroVolt included, has demonstrated net electric. Comparison is on approach and maturity, not results.

title: The Two-Machine Timeline, Side by Side
lede: Breeder and burner run on interlocking schedules — the breeder’s milestones feed directly into the burner’s, one program on two tracks.
body: MetroVolt’s schedule only makes sense next to the breeder’s. The two machines share magnets, cryogenics, controls, and helium-3, so their timelines interlock: breeder milestones are inputs to burner milestones, not parallel unrelated events.
Breeder construction (Q2 2027) seeds burner magnet, cryo, and controls experience.
Breeder first tritium (~2030) proves shared foundations and yields helium-3 coproduct.
Burner test unit (~2032) uses that experience for its first integrated run.
Commercial fleet (~2036) follows the burner test, on the FOAK–NOAK–BOAK ladder.

The dependency runs mostly one way: the breeder de-risks the burner, so breeder progress is a precondition for burner progress. This is deliberate — it lets the burner attempt the harder net-electric goal on de-risked foundations rather than from scratch.

Interlocking schedules share risk. A breeder delay does not just delay the breeder — it delays the burner that depends on it. The side-by-side view makes that coupling visible rather than hiding it in two separate roadmaps.
The two timelines are coupled. Burner dates are contingent on breeder progress, by design.

title: Readiness and Timeline FAQ
lede: Direct answers to the common honest questions about MetroVolt’s status, dates, gates, and what has and has not been demonstrated.
body: No. MetroVolt is a design and simulation study. No MetroVolt unit exists, and the burner core has not yet been built as an integrated test machine. The first integrated burner hardware is the test unit targeted near 2032.

No. No fusion machine, MetroVolt included, has demonstrated net electric output. There is no hardware net-gain claim before the breeder’s first-of-a-kind milestone, and no burner net-electric claim before the ~2032 test unit measures it.
Why is the breeder built first?

The breeder delivers value on fusion gain alone (Q_sci 3.076, 85.0 MW fusion power) and de-risks shared magnets, cryogenics, controls, and helium-3 supply. The burner then attempts the harder net-electric goal on proven foundations.
What are the biggest open questions?
Whether the tandem-mirror plug confines at feasible β (load-bearing physics).
Whether high-field plug magnets (26.49 T) can be built and sustained reliably.
Whether direct energy conversion reaches useful efficiency at scale.
Whether fleet-scale helium-3 fuel can be secured.

No. Test unit ~2032 and commercial fleet ~2036 are plan targets, contingent on breeder progress and on clearing the gates above. A failed gate moves the date; physics is not negotiated against a calendar.
MetroVolt is an honest design-stage program: strong on approach and reproducibility, explicit about what remains unproven.
